warmup.text: Last day of the week. A funny poem told as a conversation between a young man and his very strange father. Listen for two different voices, and for how calmly the father says ridiculous things.

words.text: Explain the roots in your own words, and tell what an apostrophe does in a speech spelling. In the game, the last six narrows of the week.

reading.text: Today you look back at Chapters 4, 5 and 6. Find what made you laugh, and find the one moment that is not funny at all. Then decide what the humor does for the story.

assignment.text: Three questions, the last one about the whole week. Then add one comic moment and submit your scene. Copy your work and paste it into Canvas.

game.title: Through the Strait
game.sub: This week's word game · 6 narrows today
game.look: Your ship sails west through the Strait of Magellan, a narrow passage at the bottom of South America. At each narrows, tap the channel with the word that really fits. Each narrows you pass lights a fire on Tierra del Fuego, the Land of Fire.

do: Read the clue at the narrows.
Look at the word in each channel.
Tap the channel with the word that really fits.
Tap Sail on.
how.why: A root only helps if it is really there, and a speech spelling only works if the apostrophe is in the right place.

game.doneLine: Through the Strait every day this week. Well sailed.

narrows.clue: Find the word with lude (play): a short piece played before the main event.
narrows.why: pre (before) + lude (play). Prepare comes from par, which means get ready.

narrows.clue: Find the word with lus (play): a secret plan between two people.
narrows.why: col (together) + lus (play). Collision comes from a root that means strike.
narrows.miss: One means crashing. Which one means playing together?

narrows.why: de + ris + ive: mocking. Decisive comes from cis, which means cut.

narrows.clue: Find the word with lus (play): a quick mention that plays on something the reader already knows.
narrows.why: al (toward) + lus (play) + ion. Allowance has no play root.

narrows.clue: Chapter 4: the cook shouts about what pigs are for. Which spelling is his?
narrows.a: Pigs is for eatin', not for pets.
narrows.b: Pigs is for eat'in, not for pets.
narrows.why: eatin' = eating. The apostrophe goes where the g was.

narrows.clue: Chapter 4: the cook says there is no rain in the cabin. Which spelling is his?
narrows.why: ain't is a squeezed-together word, so it needs an apostrophe. It is fine in a character's speech; spell it out in your own sentences.

art.title: The Independent Gold Hunter on His Way to California
art.alt: A hand-colored comic print of a man in tall boots walking along, loaded with a frying pan, kettle, shovel, sausages and a suitcase, with a pot on his head and a signpost behind him.
art.look: A comic print sold around 1850. The gold-seeker carries everything he owns, with a pot for a hat. The signpost says California is still 1,700 miles away, and the words under him say he will neither borrow nor lend. The artist is laughing at how sure of himself he is, the same kind of joke Fleischman makes about the gold-seekers on the Lady Wilma.
